clinicalPearls: X-linked disorder caused by the GATA1 Arg216Gln (R216Q) missense mutation in the N-terminal zinc finger of the erythroid and megakaryocyte transcription factor GATA1.

Affected males have congenital thrombocytopenia with a bleeding tendency together with a thalassaemia-like blood picture (imbalanced globin synthesis, red cell HbH-type inclusions, reticulocytosis and splenomegaly).

It is distinct from the commoner GATA1 mutations (such as V205M) that impair FOG1 (ZFPM1) binding and cause X-linked thrombocytopenia with dyserythropoietic anaemia; the R216Q allele preserves FOG1 binding but disrupts DNA binding.
Platelets are reduced in number and are structurally and functionally abnormal, so bleeding can be out of proportion to the platelet count.
Carrier females are usually mildly affected or asymptomatic, depending on X-inactivation.
The thalassaemic component can be misread as beta-thalassaemia trait; its combination with thrombocytopenia in a male-line pedigree is the clue.
Diagnosis is confirmed by GATA1 sequencing, and the family history follows an X-linked pattern.
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked thrombocytopenia with thalassaemia is caused by a specific missense mutation (Arg216Gln, R216Q) in GATA1 on the X chromosome, encoding the GATA1 transcription factor that is essential for erythroid and megakaryocytic differentiation. The substitution lies in the N-terminal zinc finger and selectively impairs binding to palindromic double-GATA DNA elements and to certain target promoters, while interaction with the cofactor FOG1 (ZFPM1) is comparatively preserved. Dysregulated globin and erythroid gene expression produces a beta-thalassaemia-like imbalance of globin chain synthesis with red cell inclusions and haemolysis, and defective megakaryopoiesis yields thrombocytopenia with structurally and functionally abnormal platelets. Other GATA1 mutations that instead disrupt FOG1 binding cause X-linked thrombocytopenia with dyserythropoietic anaemia, illustrating a genotype-phenotype correlation across the GATA1 disorders.
additionalDifferentials: GATA1-related X-linked thrombocytopenia with dyserythropoietic anaemia
Other inherited thrombocytopenias (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and X-linked thrombocytopenia from WAS, MYH9-related disorder, ANKRD26-related)
Beta-thalassaemia trait or intermedia and HbH disease (alpha-thalassaemia)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with platelet count and indices, and blood film for red cell morphology and inclusions
Reticulocyte count and markers of haemolysis
Supravital staining for HbH-type inclusions and haemoglobin analysis (HPLC or electrophoresis) with globin chain synthesis studies
Platelet function testing and platelet electron microscopy
Bone marrow examination for dysmegakaryopoiesis and dyserythropoiesis if required
Family segregation analysis consistent with X-linked inheritance
redFlags: Significant spontaneous, surgical or trauma-related bleeding
Rapidly falling platelet count or new severe anaemia
reference.prognosis: This is generally a chronic and relatively stable disorder; bleeding risk and anaemia are variable and usually manageable, but bleeding can be significant during surgery or trauma and some patients need transfusion support.
pitfalls: Diagnosing isolated beta-thalassaemia trait and missing the associated thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction, or diagnosing immune thrombocytopenia and missing the inherited thalassaemic picture.
Assuming the platelet count predicts bleeding risk when the platelets are also dysfunctional.
Missing the X-linked inheritance pattern in the family history.
Confusing it with other GATA1 disorders that carry different counselling implications.
